extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, and students using an author-date (Chicago) citation system
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing reference list entries and in-text (author–date) citations in academic writing, including structure, punctuation, ordering, and many special cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference-list entry structure
rubrics_metrics.description: In a reference list entry, the year of publication is the second element, following the author’s name. Otherwise, a reference list entry is structured like an entry in a bibliography: the elements are separated by periods, and the first-listed author’s name, according to which the entry is alphabetized in the reference list, is usually inverted (last name first).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles are capitalized headline-style unless they are in a language other than English; titles of larger works such as books and journals are italicized; titles of smaller works such as journal articles are presented in roman and enclosed in quotation marks. Noun forms such as editor, translator, volume, and edition are abbreviated, but verb forms such as edited by and translated by are spelled out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic structure of an in-text citation (author–date)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the author-date system, a citation in the text usually appears in parentheses and includes only the first two elements in a reference list—the author and the year of publication—with no intervening punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A page number or other locator may be added, following a comma. Terms such as editor or translator, abbreviated in a reference list, are omitted from a text citation. In a parenthetical reference to two or more works, a semicolon usually separates each work from the next.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page numbers and other locators
rubrics_metrics.description: In text citations where reference is usually to a particular passage, only the page numbers pertaining to that passage are given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reference lists, no page numbers are given for books; for journal articles or chapters, give the beginning and ending page numbers of the entire article or chapter. See also cross-references to other sections for locator formatting (sec., para., eq., chap., vol., etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Book with single author/editor formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: For a book with a single author, invert the name in the reference list; in the text, include only the last name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To cite a specific passage, include a page number or range in the text citation, separated from the year by a comma. Page numbers are not included in a reference list unless the entry is for a chapter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor or translator in reference list vs text citation
rubrics_metrics.description: A book with an editor in place of an author includes the abbreviation ed. (editor; for more than one editor, use eds.) in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that the text citation does not include ed. Conversely, in some cases the reference list may spell out 'Edited by' or 'Translated by' (see specific guidance) rather than abbreviate; follow the guidance for noun vs verb forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noun forms vs verb forms in abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Noun forms such as editor, translator, volume, and edition are abbreviated in reference lists; verb forms such as edited by and translated by are spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations may be used with greater frequency as long as they are used consistently (e.g., Univ., vol., no.). Some phrases like 'Edited by' or 'Translated by' should be spelled out in certain cases and capitalized if following a period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books with multiple authors
rubrics_metrics.description: For a book with two authors, only the first-listed name is inverted in the reference list. For three authors, list all names. For four or more authors, include all authors in the reference list entry; in running text cite only the first-listed author followed by et al.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word order and punctuation in the reference list are the same as for two or three authors. For in-text citations with more than three authors (or many science publications, more than two), use 'et al.' (not italicized).

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal article citation components
rubrics_metrics.description: Citations of journals typically include the volume and issue number and date of publication; the volume number follows the italicized journal title in roman and with no intervening punctuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specific page reference is included in the text; the page range for an article is included in the reference list, preceded by a colon. Record full information for the issue, including issue number even if pagination is consecutive across a volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: DOI and URL preference
rubrics_metrics.description: When the article has a DOI, the DOI is preferred to the URL that appears with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include DOI link form (https://doi.org/...) when available. For access dates and other online-source conventions see the cited sections for online materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function and placement of reference lists
rubrics_metrics.description: In the author-date system, the reference list is the prime vehicle for documentation; the text citations are merely pointers to the full list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference list is normally placed at the end of a work, preceding the index if there is one. In a multiauthor book or textbook, each chapter is usually followed by its own reference list, preceded by a subhead such as 'References' or 'Literature Cited.' Journal articles are always treated this way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetical arrangement of reference list entries
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference list is arranged alphabetically (except in a numbered reference system) and should generally not be divided into sections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All sources are listed by the last names of the authors (or, if no author or editor, by the title or a descriptive phrase). Rules for alphabetizing apply, with modifications described in related sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors’ names: recording and initials
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the authors’ names as they appear on the title page or at the head of an article or chapter, with certain exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some publications use initials rather than full given names. Chicago recommends using the form of the name as it appears in the source unless otherwise required. Make exceptions where two authors share the same initials and last name.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles in reference-list entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat titles and subtitles according to the style rules (headline-style capitalization is recommended), but recognize that some publications—particularly in the natural sciences—prefer sentence-style capitalization for titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In sentence style, only the first word and proper names are capitalized; some journals omit quotation marks or italics for article or chapter titles and abbreviate journal titles. In text, headline-style capitalization, quotation marks, and italics are the norm for English-language publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of dates in reference-list entries
rubrics_metrics.description: Because text citations consist of the last name and the year, the year in the reference list appears directly after the name, not with the publication details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the date includes month and day, the year may be repeated to avoid confusion; this arrangement facilitates easy lookup of reference list entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations usage in reference lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard bibliographic abbreviations (ed., trans., vol., no., Univ., etc.) but be consistent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spell out phrases such as 'edited by' or 'translated by' when appropriate; abbreviations may be used more frequently as long as used consistently. See related sections for months and journal abbreviations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order rules: single author vs several authors
rubrics_metrics.description: A single-author entry precedes a multiauthor entry beginning with the same name; only the first author’s name is inverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successive entries by two or more authors with the same first author are alphabetized according to the coauthors’ last names, regardless of how many coauthors there are.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and caveats of the 3-em dash for repeated names
rubrics_metrics.description: A 3-em dash can stand in for repeated reference list entries under the same name, replacing the name(s) after the first appearance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice is aimed primarily at publishers and editors; authors usually should not use the 3-em dash because it can break computerized sorts and obscure details (e.g., ed. or trans.). Publishers may choose not to apply 3-em dashes for electronic formats and databases; where dashes are not used, simply repeat author name(s) and sort normally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chronological order for successive entries by same author(s)
rubrics_metrics.description: For successive entries by the same author(s), the entries are arranged chronologically by year of publication in ascending order (a 3-em dash may replace the repeated name).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Undated works designated n.d. or forthcoming follow all dated works. If works by same two or more authors list names in a different order, the 3-em dash cannot stand in for them; they are alphabetized as if by different sets of authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: 3-em dash with edited/translated/compiled works
rubrics_metrics.description: The 3-em dash replaces preceding name(s) only, not an added ed., trans., comp., or similar abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chronological order is maintained regardless of added abbreviations; provide enough detail (ed., trans.) after the dash to indicate role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiating same-author same-year works
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more works by the same author in the same year must be differentiated by the addition of a, b, and so forth and are listed alphabetically by title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text citations consist of author and year plus letter (e.g., 2004a, 2004b). When works by same two or more authors list names in a different order, letters cannot be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement of text citation and reference-list entry
rubrics_metrics.description: For each author-date citation in the text, there must be a corresponding entry in the reference list under the same name and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author is responsible for ensuring agreement and accuracy. Specific page references in text citations must fall within the page range given in the reference list entry. Manuscript editors can help by cross-checking citations and lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text-citation basic form and punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: An author-date citation in running text or at the end of a block quotation usually consists of the last (family) name of the author, followed by the year of publication with no punctuation between author and date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abbreviations such as ed. or trans. are omitted in text citations. To refer to two or more sources in the same text citation, separate with semicolons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing authors with same last name
rubrics_metrics.description: Where two or more works by different authors with the same last name are listed, the text citation must include an initial (or two initials or a given name if necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use initials in the parenthetical citation to disambiguate (e.g., (C. Doershuk 2017) vs (J. Doershuk 2016)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Formatting page, volume, and other locators in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: When a specific page, section, equation, or other division is cited, it follows the date, preceded by a comma. When a volume as a whole is referred to, vol. is used. For volume plus page, use a colon between volume and page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (Piaget 1980, 74); (Garcia 1987, 2:345); (Fischer and Siple 1990, 212n3); for sections/paragraphs use 'sec.' or 'para.' or symbols (§) as appropriate. For works without page numbers, indicate location (e.g., heading name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional material inside parenthetical citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Parentheses that enclose a text citation may also include a comment, separated from the citation by a semicolon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (Mandolan 2017; t-tests are used here). Use square brackets if additional parentheses would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of text citations relative to punctuation
rubrics_metrics.description: Except at the end of block quotations, author-date citations are usually placed just before a mark of punctuation though need not be if the sentence would otherwise not require it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place citations where they best fit syntactically but follow the general norm of proximity to the referenced material. See exceptions for block quotations and footnotes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name used in running text
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the author’s name appears in the text, it need not be repeated in the parenthetical citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The date should immediately follow the author’s name, even if the name is used in the possessive (e.g., 'Smith’s (1999) study'). For references to a person rather than the work, include the given name on first mention if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text citations and direct quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a source citation normally follows a direct quotation, it may precede the quotation—especially if such placement allows the date to appear with the author’s name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show both placements. For block quotations, when the source is given in parentheses at the end, the opening parenthesis appears after the final punctuation mark of the quoted material; no period either precedes or follows the closing parenthesis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple references to the same source within a paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: When the same page (or page range) in the same source is cited more than once in one paragraph, the parenthetical citation can be placed after the last reference or at the end of the paragraph (but preceding the final period).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When referring to different pages in the same source within a paragraph, include a full parenthetical citation at the first reference; subsequent citations need include only page numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntactic treatment of author-date citations
rubrics_metrics.description: An author-date citation is bibliographic shorthand that corresponds to a fully cited work; it does not refer to a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions like 'in Smith 2009' outside parentheses; prefer 'in Smith (2009)' or 'in Smith’s (1999) study.' Use square brackets when parenthetical text references require additional parentheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text citations for works with many authors and disambiguation
rubrics_metrics.description: For more than three authors (or in some science publications, more than two), use the name of the first author followed by et al. in text citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a reference list includes another work of the same date that would also be abbreviated as 'X et al.' but with different coauthors or order, distinguish by citing the first two (or first three) authors followed by et al., or add a shortened title in commas to disambiguate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering multiple text references within a single parenthetical citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two or more references in a single parenthetical citation are separated by semicolons; their order may reflect what is being cited, relative importance, or (if neither applies) alphabetical or chronological order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unless a journal style prescribes an order, the decision is the author’s.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing additional works by same author(s) in a citation
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional works by the same author(s) are cited by date only, separated by commas except where page numbers are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (Whittaker 1967, 1975; Wiens 1989a, 1989b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'see also' in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Additional references prefaced by 'see also' follow any other references within a parenthetical citation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: (Guest et al. 2006; see also Stolle et al. 2008; Rahn et al. 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date system used with footnotes and endnotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Where footnotes or endnotes supplement the author-date system, source citations within notes are treated in the same way as in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Citations within notes follow the same author-date conventions illustrated for in-text citations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications preferring initials for authors’ names
rubrics_metrics.description: Some journals (especially in the natural sciences) use initials instead of given names in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When periods are used between initials, include a space (Wells, H. G.); when periods are omitted, do not place a comma between last name and initials (Wells HG). Use the form of the name as it appears with the source unless required otherwise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author-date format for anonymous works
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author/editor/translator is unknown, the reference list entry should normally begin with the title; an initial article is ignored in alphabetizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text citations may use a short form of the title (up to four words) but must include the first word (other than an initial article). Bracket a name in reference lists if authorship is known or guessed but omitted on the title page, using a question mark to indicate uncertainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of works explicitly attributed to 'Anonymous' and pseudonyms
rubrics_metrics.description: Works explicitly attributed to 'Anonymous' should be cited as Anonymous; pseudonyms are indicated in reference lists in the same manner as in bibliographies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text citations should refer to the first-listed name and omit the indication 'pseud.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor listed as author in text citations
rubrics_metrics.description: For works listed by editor(s), compiler(s), or translator(s) in a reference list, abbreviations such as ed., eds., comp., comps., or trans. following the name are omitted in text citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite the name only in text (e.g., (Silverstein 1974)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization as author
rubrics_metrics.description: If a publication is issued by an organization and carries no personal author, the organization may be listed as author in the reference list.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To facilitate shorter parenthetical citations, list the organization under an abbreviation; the entry must be alphabetized under that abbreviation (not the full name).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publications preferring sentence-style capitalization for titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications (especially in the natural sciences) prefer sentence-style capitalization for cited titles (first word and proper names only).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such usage is normally limited to the reference list; Chicago recommends headline style and the use of quotation marks/italics in both its systems, and headline-style is the norm in text for English-language publications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing works by title when no author is credited
rubrics_metrics.description: Works with no credited author are listed by title in the reference list; in text, a short version of the title (up to four words) may be used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Short forms for in-text references must include the first word of the title (aside from any article) to facilitate alphabetical lookup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reprint and modern-edition citations with original date
rubrics_metrics.description: When citing a reprint or modern edition, it is sometimes desirable to include the original date of publication; the original date is listed first, in parentheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the pagination of the original and reprint differ, indicate the edition cited. In-text parentheses containing the original date are rendered as square brackets in the citation (e.g., (Austen [1813] 2003)). When original date is less important, use date of modern source and optionally state 'First published YYYY.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Multivolume works published over multiple years
rubrics_metrics.description: When a multivolume, multiyear work is entered in the reference list, the range of dates for the work as a whole follows the author’s name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The corresponding text citation should include a volume number when referring to specific pages or volumes (e.g., (Tillich 1951-63, 1:133)). When an individual volume is listed, the date for that volume follows the name; info about the work as a whole follows info about the individual volume.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-references to multiauthor books
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid repeating information, individual contributions to an edited volume may include cross-references to an entry for the volume as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-references take the form of text citations without parentheses and are best used when many individual contributions are cited or the volume itself is cited; otherwise include full publication details for each contribution.
